Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-21
Time: 14:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes (scheduled)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Owen Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Aurora Head of ML), Daniel Brooks (Aurora Platform), Sofia Martinez (CTO)

Summary: Weekly POC sync focused on cost/unit economics. Reviewed latest tokens/sec/$ numbers from Redwood microbenchmarks, discussed caching and batching tradeoffs, clarified assumptions in Aurora's traffic profile, and aligned on next benchmark runs and deliverables.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick check-in, we have about 45 minutes, want to go over the cost numbers Owen pushed, and then decisions on batching / caching configs.
[00:18] Priya: Yep, that sounds good. we pulled some traffic snippets overnight so Daniel can share later.
[00:25] Owen: Cool, i'll start with a quick recap of the tokens per dollar metric — so the baseline we ran was the 13B quantized variant on A100-like nodes, and we get approx 2.1k tokens/sec per-dollar at 2ms p50 token, caveat this is with prefix caching off.
[00:44] Daniel: sorry, did you say 2.1k tokens per second per dollar? that seems... a bit higher than our rough estimates.
[00:52] Owen: yeah, the metric is tokens/sec/$ where the denominator is per-hour cost normalized, so it's a blended number, happy to walk through the spreadsheet. might also be that our cost model assumes reserved capacity discounts — if you want the raw on-demand numbers we have those too.
[01:10] Sofia: can you say quickly how caching changes that? we were hoping caching would give a big multiplier for our product.
[01:16] Owen: Absolutely — with prefix / KV cache enabled for repeated contexts we measured up to a 2.8x improvement in tokens/sec/$ for the particular call mix we tested (heavy reuse of product descriptions). note: the transcriber might show KV cash sometimes in the deck because the auto-captions spell it funny.
[01:36] Priya: haha, noted. so is that mainly because you avoid re-computing attention for the prefix?
[01:40] Owen: Exactly. KV cache avoids redoing the prefix tokens, and our runtime's cache hit rate assumption was set to 60% for that workload; if Aurora has a higher hit rate (say 75%) you get closer to 3.4x.
[01:55] Maya: We should call out that cache hit rate sensitivity is the biggest lever here. for customers with templated prompts it's huge; for more open-ended chat it's less.
[02:06] Daniel: Our prompts are mixed — about 40% templated instructions + 60% dynamic user input. does that map to the 60% hit rate assumption?
[02:14] Owen: it would be a reasonable starting point, yes, since the templated portion tends to be the same each call. we'll validate with your traffic sample.
[02:22] Priya: on batching — we saw your note that aggressive batching improves tokens/sec but increases p95 latency. what tradeoffs did you see?
[02:29] Owen: Right. we tested batches of 1, 4, 8, 16. tokens/sec/$ improved up to ~1.9x at batch=8 compared to batch=1, but p95 latency climbed from ~180ms to ~480ms in our 8k sequence tests. the default safe zone for Aurora's realtime UX we think is batch=4 where you get ~1.35x tokens/sec/$ and p95 still under 300ms.
[02:52] Sofia: Our SLAs are 500ms for near-real-time recommendations, so 480ms at batch=8 is borderline but maybe acceptable for offline use cases. we need to make sure fallbacks are reasonable.
[03:04] Maya: Good point — our runtime supports policy-based routing: realtime routes to lower batch / smaller model, background to larger batch / cheaper model. that can help keep user experience intact while saving cost.
[03:15] Daniel: Do you have an example of cost delta if we split 70/30 realtime/background?
[03:20] Owen: Roughly, for our test workload: pure realtime (batch=1, cache 60%) gave us ~1.2k tokens/sec/$; pure background (batch=8, cache 60%) ~2.3k tokens/sec/$. A 70/30 mix yields about 1.5k tokens/sec/$. I'll put the exact math in the spreadsheet.
[03:39] Priya: There was also a question about model variants — you mentioned quantized 13B vs float16 13B; what was the quality delta?
[03:46] Owen: In our evals quality diffs were small for your prompt set — ROUGE/embedding sim delta under 1.5% for most tasks. We recommend the 13B int8 quant for cost-savings but have a fallback to f16 for critical requests.
[03:59] Sofia: and what about running on dedicated versus hosted? our infra team is leaning dedicated (reserved GPUs) for predictable throughput.
[04:07] Maya: Dedicated does give more predictable unit costs; our dedicated pricing also includes a discounted compute unit — but up front commitment required. The spreadsheet includes a reserved capacity scenario vs hosted on-demand so you can compare.
[04:20] Daniel: can you call out networking egress and inter-region costs? that's relevant for our multi-region setup.
[04:26] Owen: Yes, egress is external to tokens/sec/$ calcs in the sheet, we have a separate tab that models egress + VPC peering charges. For your multi-region setup, routing policies can keep inference region-local to minimize egress.
[04:40] Priya: security question quickly — does caching keep customer data in the cache? we need to understand retention and encryption at rest.
[04:48] Owen: Cache entries are stored in encrypted storage and can be scoped per-tenant. retention is configurable and we can zero them on request; we also have KMS integrations for customer-managed keys in private deployments.
[05:02] Priya: good. we'll note that for procurement.
[05:06] Maya: quick aside — competitors, some folks test Anthropic and OpenAI endpoints; we've been benchmarking them too. performance numbers vary a lot by model and pricing book.
[05:16] Daniel: yeah we've seen that. price volatility on public APIs is tricky for budgeting.
[05:20] Owen: Another nuance — cold KV cache misses cause a spike in latency for the first few requests; so warm-up strategies matter for bursty traffic. We recommend a short warm-up job if you do large scale rollouts.
[05:34] Priya: helpful. about the microbenchmarks you ran — can we dive into the exact configs so we can replicate?
[05:40] Owen: Sure — we used sequence lengths 512/2k/8k, batching 1/4/8, cache hit 0/60/75, quantization int8 vs f16, and measured tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latencies, and GPU util. I'll attach the run configs and raw logs.
[05:57] Maya: We'll attach the benchmarking folder in the follow-up email (link: drive.com/redwood/aurora-benchmarks).
[06:04] Sofia: A practical ask — can you show us a simple decision tree: when to use caching, when to up batch, when to switch to smaller model?
[06:13] Owen: Yes: start with model that meets quality; enable KV cache if >30% templating reuse; if p95 latency under SLA with batch=4 keep it; if background batch=8. Switch to smaller model when unit cost target unmet but test quality drift. I'll send a one-pager.
[06:27] Priya: That will be great.
[06:30] Daniel: On instrumentation, does Redwood expose token-level cost breakdown per route? we want to map cost to features.
[06:36] Maya: Yes — Console provides token-level cost and latency per route, token breakdown, and ability to tag routes so you can bill features internally.
[06:44] Priya: Perfect.
[06:47] Owen: Quick note — our batching tradeoffs also depend on concurrency; if you have lots of concurrent users, effective batch sizes increase naturally so the perf/cost will look better.
[06:58] Daniel: Makes sense. We'll share concurrency figures.
[07:02] Priya: Looking at next steps — agree to run the 8k seq tests with our prompt set and batch=1/4/8 with cache on/off.
[07:10] Owen: I'll run those and share raw logs and a normalized cost dashboard.
[07:14] Maya: And I'll update the cost spreadsheet to show reserved vs hosted and split realtime/background scenarios.
[07:20] Sofia: Procurement will want SOC2 & KMS docs — Priya will confirm which are required.
[07:26] Maya: We'll attach security pack and SOC2 report.
[07:29] Priya: Thanks. one last question — what's the expected uplift if we also apply token compression/truncation heuristics on client side?
[07:36] Owen: In our tests simple prompt truncation and canonicalization saved ~8-12% tokens. Combined with caching that's multiplicative on dollars saved. So it's worth adding a client heuristic.
[07:48] Daniel: ok we'll prototype the client side trimming.
[07:51] Maya: Great — let's recap action items and deadlines.

Recap and next steps:
[07:55] Maya: Action items recap: Maya to send updated cost calc (due 10/25), Owen to run additional microbenchmarks (due 10/28), Daniel to share traffic/concurrency samples (due 10/26), Priya to confirm security doc needs (due 10/27). We'll schedule the benchmarking session next week.
[08:20] Sofia: Sounds good — thanks everyone.
[08:23] Priya: thanks all.
[08:25] Maya: Thanks, bye.
